item.content:encoded:
A client needed three diamond necklaces as wedding gifts for the mothers and a sister. They had been seeing retail options between $2,000 and $3,500 per necklace.

We started with CAD, sourced the diamonds, and finished all three necklaces in our Pennsylvania studio. Each features an approximately 6mm round lab-grown diamond, D or E color, VVS2 clarity, and an individual IGI grading report.

Two necklaces are in 14k yellow gold. One is in 14k white gold. The client’s price: around $900 each, or approximately $2,700 for all three.

item.title: What a wax model try-on is, and why every custom ring should have one.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.category: try on engagement ring before buying
item.description: A wax model is a wax replica of your exact ring, mailed to you to try on before anything is cast in gold. What it reveals, and what it cannot tell you.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

A wax model is a replica of your exact ring, cut in wax from the same file that will be cast in gold, and mailed to you to try on. It exists to answer the two questions a screen cannot: how the stone actually reads on that particular hand, and whether the size and proportions are right. It is the cheapest insurance in custom jewelry.

People agonize over carat weight on a screen. They compare a 1.5 against a 1.8 in renderings, read charts of millimeter spreads, and try to picture the difference. Then a wax model arrives, they put it on, and the decision takes about four seconds.

That gap between the screen and the hand is the entire reason wax models exist.

What is a wax model, exactly?

It is a physical replica of your specific ring, produced from the same digital file that will later be cast in metal. The name is not a metaphor. It is wax: the same castable wax the trade has used for a century, cut from your CAD file rather than carved by hand.

The important detail is not the material. It is that the model comes from the same CAD file that will be used for production. That is what makes it a proof rather than a mock-up. If the band on the model is 2.1 millimeters at the shoulders, the gold one will be 2.1 millimeters at the shoulders. The stone seat is where the stone will actually sit.

The model you are mailed is yours to keep. It is not the one that gets cast: when the design is approved, a fresh wax is cut from the same file, and that one goes into a flask, is surrounded by investment plaster, and is fired so the wax burns away and leaves a cavity in the exact shape of your ring. Molten gold goes into that cavity. Formlabs has a clear explanation of the lost-wax casting process. The technique is roughly 6,000 years old. Only the way the wax gets made has changed.

What does a wax model tell you that a render cannot?

Scale, profile, and fit. Three things a screen is structurally incapable of showing.

  • How big the stone actually reads on that hand. A render has no reference object. A 1.9 carat oval, which is now the average center stone size in The Knot's 2026 study, looks like a statement ring on a size 4.5 finger and looks restrained on a size 7.5. Same stone. Completely different ring. No amount of zooming tells you which one you are getting.
  • How high it sits. Profile height is the single most underrated dimension in ring design. A cathedral setting that looks elegant in a three-quarter view can be the ring that sits far higher off the finger than you pictured. Slipping the model on tells you that immediately, in a way no three-quarter render does.
  • How it fits and sits. Band width, the shape of the inside edge, and how the gallery sits against the neighbouring finger. People have strong opinions about this and almost none of them can predict those opinions in advance.

It is also a genuine sizing check. Sizing an engagement ring is harder than it sounds, especially when the ring is a surprise: GIA's ring size guide points out that the usual string-and-paper tricks are unreliable because string stretches, paper warps, and neither accounts for the knuckle the ring has to pass over. A model in the actual size settles it.

What can a wax model not tell you?

Being honest about the limits matters, because a model that is oversold disappoints:

What a wax model does and does not represent.
Accurate on the modelNot represented
Every dimension of the ringMetal color
Stone size and positionSparkle and light return
Profile height and band widthWeight in the hand
Finger size and fitSurface finish and polish
How it sits against another ringProng thickness once finished

The weight one surprises people most. Wax is close to weightless and gold is dense, so a finished platinum ring feels substantially more present on the hand than its model did. That is almost always a pleasant surprise, but it is worth knowing in advance.

Does a wax model actually change what people choose?

Most of the time, no. The design is already right, and the model says so. That is not a wasted step. Walking into a proposal certain about the ring is most of what the try-on is for.

When it does change something, the direction surprises people: they go smaller on the center stone, not larger. What happens is that the number stops being abstract. On a spreadsheet, 2.2 carats sounds better than 1.8 because it is a bigger number, and lab grown pricing means the jump often costs less than people assume. On the hand, the 1.8 sometimes just looks more like the person wearing it.

That is the whole case for the step. It usually costs you a week and buys certainty, and occasionally it catches the one thing a screen was never going to show you.

Does it add time or cost?

About a week, almost entirely mail time, and at Ring Mint there is no separate charge for it. Cutting the wax itself takes hours and the try-on takes a minute. The week is shipping the model out and getting your feedback back into a revised design.

If a proposal date is tight, this is the step that gets cut first, and cutting it is a real trade-off rather than a formality. It is worth building the extra week into the schedule from the start if you can. Our guide to how long a custom engagement ring takes lays out where that week fits.

Should you ask for one?

Ask if any of the following is true. Skip it if none of them are:

  • You are undecided between two stone sizes, or between two carat weights within about half a carat.
  • The ring has to sit flush against an existing wedding band.
  • The wearer works with their hands, or has said anything about rings catching on things.
  • You are guessing at the ring size rather than knowing it.
  • The design is unusual: an off-catalog shape, an heirloom stone, or an asymmetric setting.

If you are having a stock solitaire made in a size you have confirmed, a model is a nice-to-have rather than a necessity. Note that a wax try-on is only possible at all when a file of your specific ring exists, which is to say only on genuinely custom work. A configurator cannot print you a model of a setting that is already sitting in a warehouse.

One thing from the bench: it is real wax, and wax breaks. Try it on, look at your hand, take it off. The answer arrives in the first few seconds. Then keep it, or break it, it does not matter: the wax that gets cast is a fresh one, cut from the same file when the design is approved. Clients keep them more often than not.

Related reading

  • How a custom engagement ring is designed and made, including where the wax step sits in the process.
  • Custom versus customizable, and why only one of the two can produce a wax model of your ring.
  • Straight answers on sizing, timelines, and what happens if the fit is wrong.

Quick answers

What is a wax model ring?

A wax model is a physical replica of a specific custom ring, produced from the same CAD file that will be used to cast the finished piece. It is real castable wax, the same material the trade has used for a century, cut from your file rather than carved by hand. Ring Mint sends one on request, so the ring can be tried on and assessed before any metal is cast. Wax is fragile, so it is meant for a brief try-on rather than for wearing, and the client keeps it: a fresh wax is cut for the actual casting.

Is a wax model the same size as the real ring?

Yes. Every dimension is identical, because it is cut from the file that will be cast: stone size and position, band width, profile height, and finger size. What it does not represent is metal color, sparkle, weight, or final surface finish, since wax is close to weightless and does not reflect light the way polished gold does.

Does a wax model try-on cost extra?

At Ring Mint there is no separate charge for a wax model, and there is no concierge fee either. Practices vary across the trade, so it is worth asking any jeweler directly whether a model is included, billed separately, or not offered at all.

How much time does a wax model add to a custom ring?

Roughly a week, and it is almost all mail time. Cutting the wax takes hours and the try-on itself takes a minute. The week is shipping the model out and getting your feedback back into a revised design. If a proposal date is tight this is usually the first step to be cut, so it is better to build the week in from the start.

Can I get a wax model of a ring from a ring builder?

No. A wax model can only be made when a CAD file of your specific ring exists, which means the ring has to have been designed from scratch. Ring builders assemble stones into settings that already exist as finished stock, so there is no per-client file to cut a wax from.

item.title: Toi et moi engagement rings: how to design one that actually works.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.description: Two stones on one band is the fastest-growing ring style and the easiest to get wrong. Pairing, ratio, height, and the wedding band problem nobody mentions.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

A toi et moi ring sets two stones side by side on one band, and the name is French for "you and me". It is the fastest-growing engagement ring style and the easiest one to get wrong, because two stones have to be in conversation rather than competition. Four decisions determine which of those you get.

Toi et moi is having its moment. It is the most saved, most requested two-stone style in bridal right now, and it is the design I most often have to talk people through carefully, because the failure mode is not obvious until the ring exists.

A solitaire has one job. A toi et moi has two stones that have to relate to each other, and the relationship is the whole design. Get it right and the ring reads as one idea. Get it wrong and it reads as two rings that collided.

What is a toi et moi ring?

Two centre stones set side by side on a single band, usually with the shank splitting and curving so each stone sits on its own arm. The name is French for "you and me", and the symbolism is the obvious one: two people, one ring.

It is a genuinely old style rather than a recent invention, and it has moved in and out of fashion for a couple of centuries. GIA lists it among the standard setting styles, alongside solitaire, halo and three stone, which is a reasonable signal that it has stopped being a novelty.

Worth distinguishing from its neighbours. A three stone ring has a dominant centre with two smaller flanking stones and reads as symmetrical. A bypass ring has a shank that crosses over itself, which a toi et moi often uses but does not require. A toi et moi has two stones of comparable importance, and that parity is what makes it hard.

Decision one: matching or contrasting?

There are really only two coherent strategies, and the trouble starts when a design lands between them.

  • Matched. Two stones of the same shape, size and colour. Calm, symmetrical, and it reads as deliberate from across a room. The risk is that it can look like a stock design, and matched pairs cost more to source because the two stones genuinely have to match.
  • Deliberately contrasting. Two different shapes, or two different colours, or both. An oval with a pear. A diamond with a teal sapphire. This is where the style gets interesting and where most of the demand is.

What does not work is nearly matching. Two ovals that are almost the same size, or two whites that are almost the same colour, look like a mistake rather than a choice. The eye is extremely good at spotting near-misses and very forgiving of obvious differences. If you are going to contrast, contrast properly.

Decision two: the ratio

Either equal, or clearly unequal. Around 60:40 by spread is the sweet spot for asymmetry.

Equal sizing gives you balance and reads as a partnership of equals, which is often the point. Unequal sizing gives you a focal point and a supporting stone, which tends to photograph better and to suit a smaller hand, since two full-size stones side by side can span an entire finger.

The trap is the middle. A 1.5 carat next to a 1.3 carat is not obviously either. It looks like someone tried to match and failed. If you want asymmetry, make it visible: a 1.5 next to a 0.9 is a design, not an error.

Note that carat weight is the wrong unit for this decision. Two stones of different shapes at identical carat weights can look very different in size, because shapes carry weight differently. A one carat oval spreads considerably wider than a one carat round. Judge the pairing on millimetre spread, and ideally on a wax model rather than a screen.

Decision three: height and orientation

This is the one that gets skipped, and it is the one that ruins rings.

Two stones of different shapes have different depths. A pear and an emerald cut of the same spread will not naturally sit with their tables at the same height, and if you set them without accounting for it, one stone catches the light while the other sits in shadow. From directly above it looks fine. From every other angle, which is every angle a ring is actually seen from, one stone is doing the work.

The fix is unglamorous and entirely a matter of the setting: the seats are cut to different depths so the tables finish level. It requires a setting designed around those two specific stones, which is precisely why this style is difficult to buy off a shelf.

Orientation is the smaller sibling of the same problem. Two stones can sit parallel along the finger, angled toward each other, or one east-west and one north-south. Angled tends to feel more organic, parallel more formal. It is worth seeing both before deciding.

Decision four: the wedding band problem

A toi et moi will not sit flush against a straight wedding band, and almost nobody mentions this before the ring is made.

A solitaire has a single stone above the centre of the band, so a straight band tucks neatly underneath. A toi et moi spreads its mass across two points, and the shank usually curves or bypasses to get there. Push a straight band against it and you get a visible gap, or the band sits at an angle, or it rubs the underside of a stone every day for a decade.

There are three solutions, and it is much better to choose one now than in two years:

  1. A contoured band designed against the actual engagement ring, which is the usual answer and the best-looking one.
  2. Wear the band on the other hand, which more people do than you would think.
  3. Design the engagement ring with a flat underside from the start, accepting a slightly less fluid look in exchange for band compatibility.

All three require the ring to be designed rather than selected, which is the recurring theme with this style. It is one of the clearest cases where a configurator simply cannot get you there.

What does a toi et moi cost?

Roughly what two stones cost, plus a setting that is more work than a solitaire. There is no magic premium for the style itself, but there are two real cost drivers.

First, you are buying two centre stones instead of one, so a matched pair at a given size costs close to double a single stone of that size, not double the price of a stone half the weight. Second, matched pairs carry a sourcing premium: finding two stones that agree on colour, cut and proportion takes longer than finding one good stone, and dealers price that.

The counterintuitive move is that contrasting designs are often cheaper than matched ones, because you are not paying the matching premium and because a coloured stone paired with a diamond can cost far less than a second diamond. A diamond and sapphire pairing frequently lands below the price of two comparable diamonds, and looks more distinctive doing it.

One thing from the bench: the most successful toi et moi rings I have made have all had a reason for the pairing that had nothing to do with fashion. Two birthstones. A family diamond next to a new one. A stone from each side. The design carries meaning easily, and rings that carry meaning tend to survive the trend cycle that made them popular.

Related reading

  • How a custom ring gets designed and made, from brief to insured delivery.
  • Why a wax model matters more here than usual, when two stones have to balance on one hand.
  • Custom versus customizable, and why this style falls firmly on one side of that line.

Quick answers

What is a toi et moi engagement ring?

A toi et moi ring sets two centre stones side by side on a single band, usually with the shank splitting or bypassing so each stone sits on its own arm. The name is French for "you and me", and the two stones are traditionally read as representing the two people. GIA lists it among standard engagement ring setting styles alongside solitaire, halo and three stone.

What is the difference between a toi et moi and a three stone ring?

A three stone ring has one dominant centre stone with two smaller flanking stones and reads as symmetrical around that centre. A toi et moi has two stones of comparable importance and no single centre, which is what makes the relationship between them the whole design. A bypass ring describes the shank crossing over itself, which a toi et moi often uses but does not require.

Should the two stones in a toi et moi be the same size?

Either clearly the same or clearly different. Equal sizing reads as a partnership of equals; a ratio of roughly 60:40 by millimetre spread gives you a focal point and a supporting stone. What fails is the middle ground, where two stones are almost but not quite matched and the ring looks like an error rather than a choice. Judge the pairing on spread rather than carat weight, since different shapes carry weight differently.

Can you wear a wedding band with a toi et moi ring?

Not a straight one, comfortably. A toi et moi spreads its mass across two points and usually has a curved or bypassing shank, so a straight band leaves a visible gap, sits at an angle, or rubs against a stone. The usual solution is a contoured band designed against the actual ring, which means it has to be made rather than bought. Some people wear the band on the other hand instead.

Is a toi et moi ring more expensive than a solitaire?

Usually, because you are buying two centre stones rather than one, and a matched pair carries a sourcing premium since two stones have to agree on colour, cut and proportion. Contrasting designs are often cheaper than matched ones, and pairing a diamond with a coloured stone such as a sapphire frequently costs less than two comparable diamonds.

item.title: Ring Mint and Ring Concierge: two different companies, two different models.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.description: Similar names, unrelated businesses. One is a New York fine jewelry brand with four stores. The other is a one-person custom concierge with none.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

They are unrelated companies that happen to have similar names. Ring Concierge is a New York fine jewelry brand founded in 2013, with four stores and a bridal showroom. Ring Mint is a one-person custom concierge founded in 2025, with no store at all. If you want to walk in and try things on, you want the first. If you want a ring drawn from scratch with no retail overhead in the price, that is the second.

Ring Mint gets search traffic from people looking for Ring Concierge. That is entirely because the names are similar, and it seems more useful to write the comparison honestly than to quietly benefit from the confusion.

Disclosure up front: Ring Mint wrote this, and Ring Mint is one of the two companies in it. Everything below about Ring Concierge comes from their own published information, linked so you can check it. There is no affiliation, partnership or connection between the two businesses.

Who is who?

Ring Concierge was founded in 2013 by Nicole Wegman and is based in New York. Their about page lists fine jewelry stores in Soho and on Madison Avenue in New York, at Westfield Century City in Los Angeles, and at Town Center in Boca Raton, plus a bridal showroom in Midtown Manhattan by appointment. They sell ready-to-wear fine jewelry, including a signature tennis collection, alongside engagement rings and wedding bands, and they offer an online ring builder.

Ring Mint was founded in 2025 by Chloe Alpert, a second-generation jeweler who has worked in the trade since 2009 and grew up in her mother's business, Teaman Jewelry, founded in 1979. There is no store, no showroom, no employees and no held inventory. Every piece is designed from scratch and made to order, with stones sourced only after a client describes what they want. The founder background is here and every client review is here.

The names are a coincidence. "Ring concierge" is also a generic description of a service, which is part of why the collision happens at all.

How the two models differ

Ring Concierge and Ring Mint, compared on published information as of September 2026.
Ring ConciergeRing Mint
Founded20132025
FounderNicole WegmanChloe Alpert
BaseNew YorkPennsylvania
Physical storesFour, plus a bridal showroomNone
Held inventoryYes, ready-to-wearNone
Try on in personYesBy mailed wax model
Team sizeA companyOne person
Who you talk toA specialistThe founder
Beyond bridalFull ready-to-wear collectionsMade to order only

Neither column is the better one. They are answers to different questions.

When Ring Concierge is the better choice

Genuinely, and this is not a courtesy paragraph:

  • You want to try rings on in a store. Nothing replaces putting a finished ring on a hand under real light, and if you are in New York, Los Angeles or Boca Raton you can do exactly that.
  • You want to buy something today. A brand with inventory can hand you a finished piece. A made-to-order business structurally cannot.
  • You want the brand. That is a real thing to want. A recognised name has value to some people and pretending otherwise would be silly.
  • You are shopping for ready-to-wear fine jewelry rather than a commissioned piece.
  • You were looking for their careers page or customer service. Ring Mint cannot help with either. Go to ringconcierge.com directly.

When a business like Ring Mint is the better choice

  • The ring you want is not in anyone's catalog. An heirloom stone in a non-standard size, a band that has to sit flush against an existing ring, an asymmetric setting. These are the cases where a ring builder runs out of road.
  • You want the overhead out of the price. A store pays for a lease, a sales floor and every piece in the case that did not sell, and all of it is recovered in what does sell. Ring Mint clients typically pay 30 to 50 percent less than the retail price of a comparable ring for that reason alone.
  • You would rather text than book an appointment. Most of the process here happens over WhatsApp.
  • You want one person accountable end to end, from the first question to the insured delivery, rather than a handoff between departments.

Where Ring Mint is genuinely weaker

A comparison written by one of the parties is worth nothing without this section.

  • You cannot walk in. There is no showroom, anywhere, and there is not going to be one. A wax model mailed to your door is the substitute, and it is a good one, but it is not the same as a tray of finished rings.
  • Nothing is available immediately. Everything is made to order, so the floor is about three weeks. If you need a ring next Tuesday, Ring Mint is the wrong call and will say so.
  • It is one person. That is the appeal for many clients and a real constraint for others. Capacity is finite, and August is not January.
  • The track record is shorter. Ring Concierge has been operating since 2013. Ring Mint launched in 2025, on the back of a family business running since 1979, which is not the same thing as a decade of its own trading history. The reviews page shows everything there is, unedited.

How to choose, in one question

Does the ring you want already exist?

If yes, or close enough that a small adjustment would do it, buy it from someone who has it. You will get it faster and you will get to try it on first. That is a good outcome and there is no reason to overcomplicate it.

If no, and you keep finding rings that are almost right, then no amount of browsing will fix that, and the answer is to have one drawn. That is the whole reason a business like Ring Mint exists.

One thing from the bench: I have told people to go buy a ring somewhere else more than once, usually because their deadline was too close or because they had already found something they loved. It costs a sale and it is obviously the right call. A ring nobody is happy with is worse for everybody than a sale I did not make.

Related reading

  • What an engagement ring concierge actually does, and how it compares to a configurator or a showroom.
  • Custom versus customizable, the distinction underneath this whole comparison.
  • Every Ring Mint review, in full, linked to the verified originals.

Quick answers

Is Ring Mint the same company as Ring Concierge?

No. They are unrelated businesses with similar names and no affiliation, partnership or shared ownership. Ring Concierge was founded in 2013 by Nicole Wegman and is based in New York with four stores and a bridal showroom. Ring Mint was founded in 2025 by Chloe Alpert in Pennsylvania and has no store, showroom or inventory at all.

What is the difference between Ring Mint and Ring Concierge?

Ring Concierge is a fine jewelry brand that holds inventory, sells ready-to-wear collections alongside bridal, operates physical stores in New York, Los Angeles and Boca Raton, and offers an online ring builder. Ring Mint is a one-person made-to-order concierge with no retail presence, which designs every piece from scratch and sources stones only after a client describes what they want.

Which should I choose for an engagement ring?

Ask whether the ring you want already exists. If it does, or something close enough does, buy from a brand that stocks it: you will get it faster and can try it on first. If you keep finding rings that are almost right, particularly if an heirloom stone or a fitted wedding band is involved, a ring designed from scratch is the answer and browsing will not get you there.

I was looking for Ring Concierge's careers page or customer service.

Ring Mint cannot help with either, since they are separate companies. Go to ringconcierge.com directly for their jobs, orders and customer service.

What are the drawbacks of using Ring Mint instead of a store?

There is no showroom to visit, so trying on happens through a wax model mailed to you rather than a tray of finished rings. Nothing is available immediately, since everything is made to order with a floor of about three weeks. It is one person, so capacity is finite. And the company launched in 2025, so its own trading history is short, even though the founder has been in the trade since 2009.

Decided it is the custom route?

Ring Mint designs from scratch, sources against your brief rather than from a case, and carries no store, showroom or inventory. Email Chloe. If it turns out you want something else, you will be told that too.

item.title: Lab diamond vs. moissanite: the honest comparison.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.category: difference between moissanite and lab diamond
item.description: One is a diamond and one is not. What actually separates them, how to tell them apart, and why falling lab prices have eaten most of moissanite's case.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

A lab grown diamond is a diamond. Moissanite is not. Moissanite is silicon carbide, a different mineral with different optics, and it throws noticeably more rainbow fire as a result. Both are legitimate choices when honestly described. What has changed is the money: lab diamond prices have fallen so far that moissanite's main argument has largely evaporated.

This comparison usually gets written by someone selling one of the two, which is why it usually reaches a confident conclusion. I sell both, and I think the honest answer depends almost entirely on your budget and on how you feel about rainbows.

What is the actual difference?

They are different minerals. That is not a technicality, it is the whole thing.

A lab grown diamond is carbon arranged in a cubic crystal lattice. So is a mined diamond. They are the same material with the same hardness, the same optical properties, and the same behaviour, distinguishable only by trace growth features that a laboratory can see and you cannot. Moissanite is silicon carbide: silicon and carbon in a hexagonal structure. GIA classes it among diamond simulants, materials that "are completely unrelated to diamonds at the atomic level."

Lab grown diamond and moissanite compared.
Lab grown diamondMoissanite
MaterialCarbonSilicon carbide
Is it a diamond?YesNo
Mohs hardness10About 9.25
Dispersion (fire)0.0440.104
Refractive behaviourSingly refractiveDoubly refractive
Sold byCarat weightUsually millimetre size
Graded by IGI or GIAYesNot on the 4Cs

Two rows there do the real work. Dispersion of 0.104 against 0.044 means moissanite splits light into spectral colours more than twice as strongly as diamond, which is the source of its distinctive rainbow flash. And double refraction means light entering the stone splits into two rays, so facet edges appear doubled when you look through it at an angle. In a small stone this is invisible. Past about a carat and a half it becomes something you can see.

How do you tell them apart?

Not by eye, reliably, and not with a cheap thermal tester either. This trips up more people than anything else in the category.

Old diamond testers measure thermal conductivity, and moissanite conducts heat similarly enough to diamond that it passes. Testers sold as combination diamond and moissanite testers add an electrical conductivity check, which does separate them, but only if the seller owns one and uses it.

The reliable tells are optical: look through the table at a shallow angle under magnification and moissanite shows doubled facet junctions, and under most lighting it throws more coloured fire than a diamond of the same size. In practice, though, the answer for a buyer is paperwork. A lab grown diamond comes with an IGI report tied to a laser inscription on the girdle. Moissanite does not. If a stone is being sold as a lab diamond and there is no report, treat the claim as unsupported.

That is not a hypothetical. We bought more than fifty stones advertised as lab grown diamonds from over twenty eBay sellers, and every single one was moissanite, most with a coating on the pavilion that polished off. Moissanite is a perfectly good product. Moissanite sold as a diamond is fraud.

Does moissanite still make financial sense?

Less than it used to, and this is the part most comparisons have not caught up with.

The case for moissanite was never optical. It was that you could have a large, bright, durable stone for a small fraction of a diamond's price. That argument was overwhelming in 2018, when a two carat lab grown diamond was still expensive.

Lab grown diamond prices have since fallen by something like 80 to 90 percent from their 2020 levels, and they now sit close to a production-cost floor. A one carat lab grown round in a decent quality is a few hundred dollars at wholesale. Moissanite has not fallen nearly as far, because it was already cheap and its price was never being propped up by the same dynamics. The gap between the two has narrowed from a chasm to a step.

Which means the question has changed. It used to be "can you afford a diamond?" It is now closer to "do you prefer more fire, or do you prefer the word diamond and a grading report?" Both are legitimate answers, but the second one now costs much less than people assume.

Which one actually looks better?

Genuinely a matter of taste, and people are unusually consistent once they see them side by side. Moissanite is showier. It throws more coloured light, and in bright sun or under restaurant spotlights it does something diamond does not: a visible spray of rainbow. Some people find that spectacular and some find it reads as costume.

Diamond returns more of its light as white brilliance with flashes of colour rather than sheets of it. It is the more restrained of the two.

My advice is to look at both in daylight rather than in a jewelry store, because retail lighting is engineered to make everything look like moissanite. And note that the difference scales with size. At half a carat almost nobody can tell. At three carats almost anybody can.

What about durability?

Both are fine for daily wear, and the gap is smaller than the numbers suggest. Diamond is 10 on the Mohs scale and moissanite about 9.25, but the scale is not linear and both sit far above anything they will meet in ordinary life. Neither will scratch from normal wear.

The more relevant property is toughness, meaning resistance to chipping, and here both have the same real vulnerability: an exposed girdle or a sharp corner struck at the wrong angle. A pear or marquise tip is the usual casualty. That is a setting problem, not a material problem, which is why a protective bezel or a well-designed prong matters more than which stone you chose.

So which should you choose?

  • Choose a lab grown diamond if you want a graded, inscribed stone, if the word diamond matters to you or to the person wearing it, or if you want the more restrained look. At current prices this is affordable for most budgets that would previously have ruled it out.
  • Choose moissanite if you love the extra fire, if you want the largest possible stone for a very tight budget, or if you want something for travel or for a piece that will take hard wear.
  • Do not choose an unlabelled stone from a marketplace listing on the promise that it is a lab diamond.

If you want the fuller picture on the diamond side, including how lab stones are grown and what resale actually looks like, that is on our lab created diamond engagement rings page. And if you are weighing certification, the IGI and GIA question changed in 2025 in a way most guides have not updated for.

One thing from the bench: the clients who end up happiest with moissanite are the ones who chose it deliberately, usually because they liked the fire. The ones who end up disappointed almost always chose it as a compromise. At today's lab diamond prices, that compromise is rarely necessary any more, and it is worth pricing the diamond version before assuming it is out of reach.

  • IGI vs. GIA for lab grown diamonds, and why the answer changed in 2025.

Quick answers

Is moissanite a diamond?

No. Moissanite is silicon carbide, a different mineral from diamond, which is carbon. GIA classifies moissanite as a diamond simulant, a material that imitates a diamond's appearance but is unrelated to it at the atomic level. A lab grown diamond, by contrast, is chemically and structurally a real diamond.

Can a diamond tester tell moissanite from a lab diamond?

Not a basic one. Traditional testers measure thermal conductivity, and moissanite conducts heat closely enough to diamond that it passes as one. Combination testers that also measure electrical conductivity do separate them. The dependable check for a buyer is paperwork: a lab grown diamond comes with an IGI report tied to a laser inscription on the girdle, and moissanite does not.

Does moissanite look different from a diamond?

Yes, and the difference grows with size. Moissanite has roughly 2.4 times the dispersion of diamond, so it splits light into spectral colours much more strongly and produces a visible rainbow flash. It is also doubly refractive, meaning facet edges appear doubled when viewed through the stone at an angle. Below about half a carat almost nobody can tell; above two carats most people can.

Is moissanite cheaper than a lab grown diamond?

Yes, but by far less than it used to be. Lab grown diamond prices have fallen roughly 80 to 90 percent since 2020 and now sit close to a production-cost floor, while moissanite prices have not fallen nearly as far because they were already low. The gap that once made moissanite the obvious budget choice has narrowed considerably.

Is moissanite durable enough for an engagement ring?

Yes. Moissanite is about 9.25 on the Mohs hardness scale against diamond's 10, and both sit far above anything encountered in daily life, so neither scratches from ordinary wear. The real risk for both is chipping at an exposed girdle or a sharp corner, such as the tip of a pear or marquise, which is a question of how the stone is set rather than what it is made of.

item.title: IGI vs. GIA for lab grown diamonds: what changed, and which report to get.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.category: which lab diamond certificate is best
item.description: GIA stopped grading lab diamonds on the 4Cs and now issues Premium or Standard instead. What that means for buyers, and why IGI is the practical choice.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

For a lab grown diamond in 2026, IGI is the practical choice, and the reason has nothing to do with strictness. GIA stopped applying the 4Cs to lab grown stones in late 2025. It now issues a two-tier assessment, Premium or Standard. If you want to know that your stone is F colour and VS1 clarity, IGI is the only major lab that will still tell you.

Most articles comparing IGI and GIA are out of date, and they are out of date in a way that matters. They will tell you that GIA is the stricter lab, that IGI runs about a grade looser on colour and clarity, and that you should therefore expect to pay more for a GIA-graded stone of the same stated quality.

All of that was true. For lab grown diamonds it is now beside the point, because GIA no longer issues colour and clarity grades for lab grown diamonds at all.

What changed at GIA?

In 2025 GIA announced that it would stop applying the 4Cs nomenclature to laboratory-grown diamonds and move to descriptive terminology instead. In GIA's own words, announcing the change: "More than 95% of laboratory-grown diamonds entering the market fall into a very narrow range of color and clarity. Because of that, it is no longer relevant for GIA to describe man-made diamonds using the nomenclature created for the continuum of color and clarity of natural diamonds."

What replaced it is a Laboratory-Grown Diamond Quality Assessment with two possible outcomes, Premium and Standard, awarded on an overall review of colour, clarity and finish rather than as separate letter and number grades. And there is a third outcome that gets less attention: a stone that fails to reach the minimum threshold receives no designation at all.

The logic is defensible. The 4Cs scale was built to describe natural diamonds, which vary enormously because geology is not a controlled process. A CVD reactor is a controlled process, and the output clusters tightly. Applying a scale with 23 colour grades to a population that mostly occupies four of them arguably implies a precision that is not doing any work.

Whether you agree or not, the practical consequence is the same.

So which report should you get?

For a lab grown diamond, IGI. IGI continues to grade lab diamonds on the full 4Cs, with a colour grade, a clarity grade, a cut grade, and measurements. If you want to compare two stones on anything finer than a two-tier bucket, that is the report that lets you.

What each lab now provides, by stone type.
IGIGIA
Lab grown: colour gradeYes, full scaleNo
Lab grown: clarity gradeYes, full scaleNo
Lab grown: overall verdictImplied by the gradesPremium or Standard
Lab grown: below thresholdStill gradedNo designation issued
Natural: 4Cs gradingYesYes, the industry standard
Share of lab grown marketThe large majoritySmall

For a natural diamond, none of this applies and GIA remains the reference standard. That has not changed and is unlikely to.

Is IGI really looser than GIA?

Historically yes, by roughly a grade on colour and clarity, and it matters less than the internet suggests. The comparison is only meaningful when the same stone could plausibly go to either lab, which for lab grown diamonds is now rarely the case.

Where the "looser" reputation still bites is in cross-shopping. If you compare an IGI F VS1 against a GIA-graded natural F VS1 and conclude the lab stone is a bargain, you are comparing two different scales as though they were one. Compare lab against lab.

The more useful point is that a grade is a description, not an endorsement. A stone can hold excellent paper grades and still look wrong: strong blue fluorescence that reads as milky in daylight, a cut that meets its grade on paper while leaking light through the pavilion, or a nominally eye-clean clarity where the inclusion happens to sit directly under the table. We wrote about the low end of this market in our piece on whether TikTok auction diamonds are real. The short version is that they are real, and that being real is not the same as being good.

Does the lab affect resale value?

Marginally, and it is the wrong thing to optimise for. Lab grown diamond resale is poor regardless of which lab graded the stone, because wholesale prices have fallen so far that a stone bought two years ago is competing against new production at a fraction of what it cost. Natural diamonds also resell well below retail. Neither is an investment, and any jeweler who tells you otherwise is selling something.

Buy the stone you want to look at. The full argument, with numbers, is on our lab created diamond engagement rings page.

How to actually read the report you have

Whichever lab issued it, four things are worth more of your attention than colour:

  • The report number, verified on the lab's own site. Look it up yourself before buying, not after. A report is a photograph of a specific stone, and the only thing tying it to the stone in front of you is that number, usually laser-inscribed on the girdle.
  • Cut grade and the measurements together. A one carat round should measure roughly 6.4 to 6.5 millimetres across. Meaningfully smaller means the weight is hidden in the depth where it does nothing for you.
  • Fluorescence. Usually irrelevant, occasionally the reason a stone looks hazy in daylight. Strong is worth a second look.
  • The plotted inclusions, not just the clarity letter. Where an inclusion sits matters more than what grade it produced.

One thing from the bench: I have rejected stones with better paper than the ones I ended up buying, more than once. The report tells you what is measurable. It does not tell you how the stone behaves when you tilt it under an ordinary kitchen light, which is where an engagement ring actually lives.

Related reading

  • Lab created diamond engagement rings, explained honestly, including how they are grown and what resale really looks like.
  • What happens with no report at all: we bought 50 "lab diamonds" on eBay and every one was moissanite.
  • Straight answers on certification, appraisal and what ships with every ring.

Quick answers

Does GIA still grade lab grown diamonds on the 4Cs?

No. GIA moved to descriptive terminology for laboratory-grown diamonds and now issues a Laboratory-Grown Diamond Quality Assessment with a two-tier designation, Premium or Standard, based on an overall review of colour, clarity and finish. Individual colour and clarity grades are no longer issued for lab grown stones. Natural diamonds continue to receive full 4Cs grading.

Is IGI or GIA better for a lab grown diamond?

IGI, for a practical reason rather than a quality one. IGI still grades lab grown diamonds on the full 4Cs, so you get a colour grade, a clarity grade, a cut grade and measurements you can compare between stones. GIA now gives lab stones only a Premium or Standard designation, which is a two-tier bucket rather than a scale.

What happens if a lab diamond does not meet GIA's minimum standard?

It receives no designation at all. GIA states that a man-made diamond that fails to achieve the minimum standard for quality will not be given a designation, so the absence of a GIA assessment on a stone is itself information.

Is IGI grading less strict than GIA?

Historically IGI has run roughly one grade looser than GIA on colour and clarity. That comparison matters most when cross-shopping between a lab grown stone and a natural one, where you would be comparing two different scales. Compare lab grown stones against other lab grown stones, and treat any grade as a description of the stone rather than an endorsement of it.

Does the grading lab affect a lab diamond's resale value?

Only marginally, and resale is the wrong thing to optimise for with a lab grown stone. Wholesale lab diamond prices have fallen steeply, so a stone bought a couple of years ago competes against new production at a fraction of its original cost, whichever lab graded it. Natural diamonds also resell well below retail.

item.title: How long does a custom engagement ring take?
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.category: how long does a custom engagement ring take
how long to make an engagement ring
item.description: About two weeks to manufacture, and three to six weeks start to finish. Where the time actually goes, what makes it slower, and how to hit a proposal date.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

About two weeks to manufacture once a design is approved, and three to six weeks from the first conversation to a ring in your hand. Manufacturing is the predictable part. The variable is the design phase, which depends almost entirely on how quickly you make decisions, not on how fast a workshop can work.

The honest answer is that a custom engagement ring takes about three to six weeks, and that almost nobody's ring takes exactly that, because the number is dominated by a stage most people do not think of as part of the schedule.

Making the ring is the reliable part. Two weeks, give or take, and a workshop can plan around it. Deciding what the ring is can take an afternoon or it can take a month, and that is the number that actually moves.

How long does each stage take?

Here is the full sequence with realistic durations. Note that sourcing and design overlap rather than running in sequence, which is why the totals are shorter than the sum of the parts.

Custom engagement ring stages and realistic durations.
StageTypicalFastestWhat drives it
First conversation and brief1 to 3 daysSame dayYour availability
Stone sourcing2 to 7 days1 dayHow specific or rare the stone is
CAD design and revisions1 to 3 weeks2 daysHow many rounds you want
Wax model try-on (optional)1 weekSkippedMail time each way
ManufacturingAbout 2 weeks7 to 10 daysCasting, setting, finishing
Appraisal, photos, shipping3 to 5 days2 daysInsured transit
Total4 to 6 weeksAbout 3 weeks

Why does manufacturing take two weeks?

Because a cast ring is made in stages, and several of them cannot be hurried without showing. The printed pattern is invested in plaster, the plaster is fired so the pattern burns out, and molten metal fills the resulting cavity. That is lost-wax casting, and the burnout stage alone runs for hours in a kiln on a fixed schedule.

Then the real time begins. The casting is cut from its sprue, filed, pre-polished, and the stone seats are cut by hand. Setting a center stone and a row of pavé is slow, delicate work done under a microscope by someone who does only that. Final polishing and rhodium plating, if the piece is white gold, follow after.

Two weeks is not a queue. It is the work.

Why is the design phase the unpredictable part?

Because it moves at the speed of your decisions. The CAD work itself is fast. A first design usually comes back within a couple of days of a brief, and a revision turns around in a day. What stretches the phase is the gap between a design landing in your inbox and you deciding what you think about it.

That is not a criticism. It is a large purchase and thinking about it is reasonable. But it is worth knowing that a client who replies to each round within a day will have a finished ring roughly two weeks sooner than a client who takes a week to sit with each one, with identical work happening at the jeweler's end.

The other design-phase variable is how many rounds there are. Two or three is typical. If you are working from a clear reference image, one round sometimes does it. If you are discovering what you want as you go, which is completely normal, expect four or five. Ring Mint does not cap revisions, so this is genuinely your call rather than a billing question.

What makes a custom ring take longer?

  • A specific or rare stone. A one carat round lab diamond in a common quality can be found the same day. A 3 carat unheated Ceylon sapphire in a particular blue, or a well-cut old mine cushion, can take weeks of looking. Sourcing is the stage most likely to blow a schedule.
  • Hand engraving or milgrain. Hand work is done by a specialist, and specialists have queues. Add one to two weeks.
  • Fitting to an existing ring. If a band has to sit flush against a ring you already own, that ring usually has to be physically in the workshop or precisely scanned, which adds a shipping leg at the front.
  • A wax model try-on. About a week, almost all of it mail. Worth it in most cases.
  • December. The whole trade is busy from mid-November, so casting houses and setters run longer queues exactly when the most people want rings.

Can you hit a specific proposal date?

Yes, and that is the normal way to run the project. The schedule gets built backwards from the date rather than forwards from today, which changes what gets recommended.

With eight weeks, everything is comfortable: sourcing options, several design rounds, a wax model, and a buffer. With five weeks it still works well, usually by skipping the wax model or by being decisive about the stone early. With three weeks it is achievable but the decisions have to be quick and the stone has to be something available now rather than something being hunted.

Under three weeks the honest answer is often that a fully custom ring is the wrong tool, and that a well-chosen ready-made piece now, with a custom ring made later at a calmer pace, produces a better outcome than a rushed build. That is advice that costs Ring Mint a sale, and it is still the right advice.

How far ahead should you start?

Two months before the date you have in mind. Not because it takes two months, but because it gives you a real design phase instead of a compressed one, and because the difference between a good ring and the right ring is usually made in the rounds you would otherwise have skipped.

If you are aiming at a holiday proposal specifically, we published the order-by dates for Thanksgiving through Valentine's Day, worked out backwards from each one.

One thing from the bench: the single best thing a client can do for their own timeline is answer the budget question honestly in the first conversation. Vagueness there produces designs that have to be reworked once the real number appears, and reworking a design after the stone has been chosen is where weeks quietly disappear.

Related reading

  • The full custom engagement ring process, step by step, with what is included at each stage.
  • What a wax model try-on is, and when the extra week is worth spending.
  • Straight answers on deadlines, deposits and shipping.

Quick answers

How long does a custom engagement ring take?

About three to six weeks from the first conversation to delivery. Manufacturing accounts for roughly two weeks of that and is the most predictable stage. The rest is the brief, sourcing the stone, CAD design and revisions, an optional mailed wax model, and insured shipping with an appraisal.

What is the fastest a custom engagement ring can be made?

About three weeks, if the stone is something already available rather than something being hunted, the design is settled in one or two rounds, and the wax model try-on is skipped. Under three weeks a fully custom build starts to compromise the result, and a ready-made piece now with a custom ring later is usually the better outcome.

Why does manufacturing take two weeks?

Because a cast ring is built in stages that cannot be compressed without showing. The pattern is invested in plaster and fired so it burns out, metal is cast into the cavity, then the piece is cut from its sprue, filed, pre-polished, its stone seats cut by hand, set under a microscope, and finally polished and plated. The setting and finishing work is the bulk of it.

What slows a custom engagement ring down the most?

Two things. Sourcing an unusual stone, such as an unheated sapphire in a specific colour or a well-cut antique cushion, can take weeks of searching. And the client's own response time between design rounds, which is the single largest variable in the whole schedule.

Can a custom ring be made in time for a specific proposal date?

Usually yes, and the schedule should be built backwards from the date rather than forwards from today. Eight weeks is comfortable, five weeks works well with a decisive stone choice, and three weeks is achievable with quick decisions and an available stone. Say the date in the first conversation so the tight points get flagged before anything is committed.

item.title: Holiday proposal order-by dates for a custom ring.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.category: when to order engagement ring for christmas
item.description: The last date to start a custom engagement ring for Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year's Eve and Valentine's Day, worked backwards from each one.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

For a Christmas Day proposal, start a custom ring by November 6 to be comfortable, and by December 4 at the absolute latest. A custom ring takes three to six weeks, and the jewelry trade runs its longest queues of the year from mid-November onward. Every date below is worked backwards from the occasion, with the crunch points marked.

Engagement season is real and it is short. The stretch from Thanksgiving to Valentine's Day carries a large share of the year's proposals, and nearly nine in ten proposers pop the question with a ring already in hand, according to The Knot's 2026 study of 10,474 couples. Which means the ring has to exist before the moment does.

A custom ring takes three to six weeks. Below are the dates that follow from that, occasion by occasion.

The order-by dates

Three columns, because "the deadline" depends on what you are willing to give up. Comfortable gives you several design rounds, a mailed wax model, and a buffer. Standard works well if you are decisive and skip the model. Last call means an available stone, one or two design rounds, and no room for anything going wrong.

Dates to start a custom engagement ring, 2026 into 2027.
OccasionDateComfortableStandardLast call
ThanksgivingThu Nov 26, 2026Oct 8Oct 22Nov 5
Christmas DayFri Dec 25, 2026Nov 6Nov 20Dec 4
New Year's EveThu Dec 31, 2026Nov 12Nov 26Dec 10
Valentine's DaySun Feb 14, 2027Dec 27Jan 10Jan 24

Two of those cells deserve a warning label, and they are covered below.

Why do the December dates need a buffer?

Because everyone else wants a ring at the same time, and the people who actually make rings are a small group. From mid-November, casting houses, setters and hand engravers all run longer queues. A setting that turns around in three days in July can take eight in early December.

This is the part that catches people out. The design work is unaffected, so the process feels like it is moving normally, and then the physical making takes half again as long as it would have in the autumn. Every date in the table already includes a modest allowance for this. If you are starting inside two weeks of a last-call date, say so at the outset so the schedule can be built honestly rather than optimistically.

Shipping is the second December problem. Insured overnight carriers get slower and less reliable in the last two weeks of the month, and a ring sitting in a depot on December 23 is a genuinely bad evening. Ring Mint ships fully insured and builds transit time into the schedule, but the sane move is to have the ring in your hands several days before you need it, not the morning of.

The New Year's Eve trap

Look at the New Year's Eve row again. The standard start date is November 26, which is Thanksgiving itself, and the last call is December 10, right in the middle of the busiest fortnight of the trade's year.

New Year's Eve looks like it buys you an extra week over Christmas. In practice it does not, because the extra week is entirely consumed by the holiday slowdown, and because the workshops that would make your ring are closed for part of it. Treat a New Year's Eve proposal as though it were a Christmas one and start on the Christmas dates.

The Valentine's Day trap

The comfortable start date for Valentine's Day is December 27, which is a date on which essentially nobody in the jewelry trade is working, and on which you are probably not thinking about ring design either.

The practical version: either begin the conversation before Christmas, in the first half of December, and accept that the design phase will pause over the holidays, or plan to start properly in the first week of January and use the standard column rather than the comfortable one. Both work. What does not work is deciding on January 20 that Valentine's Day would be nice.

What if you have already missed the date?

Then do not rush a custom build, because a rushed custom ring is the one thing worse than a delayed one. There are two decent options and one bad one.

  • Propose with a placeholder and design the real ring together afterwards. This is more common than people think, it removes every deadline from the process, and it means the person wearing the ring for the next fifty years had a say in it.
  • Buy something ready-made now and make the custom piece later, as an upgrade or as a wedding band set. Ring Mint sources ready-made pieces as well as making them.
  • Compress the custom build into ten days. This is the bad one. Something will be compromised, usually the stone, because the only stones available at no notice are the ones nobody else wanted.

The date is not the point. Nobody remembers, five years later, that the proposal happened in February rather than December. They do remember the ring.

How to start, briefly

You need less than you think to begin. A rough budget and the date are genuinely enough; the stone type, shape and style can all be worked out afterwards, and working them out is the first part of the job rather than a prerequisite for it. If you have a screenshot of something you like, bring it. If you do not, that is also fine, and describing what the person is like is often more useful than a reference image anyway.

What does help enormously is knowing the ring size, or having a ring of theirs you can borrow. If neither is possible, a wax model can settle it, though that is the week you will not have if you are near a last-call date.

One thing from the bench: the busiest week of my year is the first week of December, and it is almost entirely people who assumed a ring could be made in ten days. It sometimes can. It is never the ring they would have had if they had called in October.

Related reading

  • How long a custom engagement ring takes, stage by stage, and what makes each stage slower.
  • What the custom process involves from the first conversation to insured delivery.
  • Deposits, returns and the warranty, in writing, before you commit to anything.

Quick answers

When should I order an engagement ring for a Christmas proposal?

Start a custom ring by November 6, 2026 to be comfortable, which leaves room for several design rounds and a mailed wax model. November 20 still works if you are decisive about the stone. December 4 is the last call, and it requires a stone that is already available and quick decisions on the design. The trade runs its longest queues from mid-November, so earlier is materially better.

Is New Year's Eve a safer deadline than Christmas for a custom ring?

No. New Year's Eve appears to buy an extra week over Christmas Day, but the holiday slowdown and workshop closures consume all of it. Treat a New Year's Eve proposal as though it were a Christmas one and use the Christmas dates: start by November 12 to be comfortable and December 10 at the very latest.

When should I start a custom ring for Valentine's Day 2027?

Either begin in the first half of December 2026 and accept that the design phase will pause over the holidays, or start properly in the first week of January 2027. The nominal comfortable date of December 27 falls when almost nobody in the trade is working. January 24 is the last call for February 14.

Why do engagement rings take longer to make in December?

Because casting houses, stone setters and hand engravers are all working through the year's heaviest demand at the same time. A setting that turns around in three days in July can take eight in early December. Insured shipping also slows in the last two weeks of the month, so the ring should be in your hands several days before you need it.

What should I do if I have missed the deadline for a holiday proposal?

Propose with a placeholder ring and design the real one together afterwards, or buy a ready-made piece now and commission the custom ring later. Both are better than compressing a custom build into ten days, because at that notice the only stones available are the ones nobody else selected, and the stone is the part you cannot fix later.

item.title: Custom vs. customizable: why a ring builder is not a custom ring.
item.dc:creator: Chloe Alpert
item.category: what does custom engagement ring mean
item.description: A ring builder pairs your stone with a setting that already exists. Custom means the setting is designed from scratch. What each one can and cannot do.
item.content:encoded:
The short answer

A ring builder lets you combine a stone with a setting that already exists. Fully custom means the setting itself is drawn from scratch for you, so nothing about it is fixed in advance. Both get sold as "design your own ring," but only one of them can produce a ring that does not already exist somewhere in a catalog.

Nearly every jeweler in the world advertises custom engagement rings. The word has been stretched so far that it now covers three completely different products, and the person buying a ring has no way to tell which one they are being sold until the ring shows up.

Here is the version I would give a friend. There is one question that separates the three, and it is not about price, service, or how nice the website looks. It is whether a mold for your ring already exists.

What a ring builder actually does

A ring builder is a filter over an existing catalog. You pick a setting from a menu, pick a stone from a list, and the site shows you a rendering of the two together. That is genuinely useful. It is also not design.

Everything in a builder was designed before you arrived. The prong count, the band width, the basket shape, the gallery underneath, the height the stone sits at, the way the shoulders taper: all decided, all fixed, all already cast in a mold that will be used for hundreds of other rings. Those are two separate things a builder locks down at once, incidentally. GIA's guide to ring settings draws the distinction well: a setting is how the stone is held (prong, bezel, channel), while a style is the arrangement of the whole design (solitaire, halo, three stone). Your choices are the ones the menu offers, usually metal, center stone shape, center stone size within a range, and sometimes a band width or a hidden halo toggle.

The industry term for this is semi-mount. The setting is a finished product waiting for a center stone. When a large online retailer says "build your own ring," a semi-mount is what they mean, and there is nothing dishonest about it. The dishonest part is when a small jeweler with the same catalog calls it bespoke.

What fully custom actually means

Fully custom means the setting is modeled from nothing, in CAD, for one person. There is no menu, because there is no catalog to draw from. The starting point is a conversation, and the first thing that exists is a file that did not exist yesterday.

What that changes in practice: the band can be any width at any point along its length. The stone can sit at any height. The basket can be shaped around a specific finger, or around a specific wedding band that has to sit flush against it. A side stone can be a family diamond that is 4.1 millimeters when every catalog setting expects 4.0. The gallery can carry an engraving nobody else will ever see.

None of that is exotic. It is just what happens when the geometry is drawn to fit rather than picked from a list.

What about semi-custom?

Semi-custom is a real category and it is where most "custom" jewelers actually operate. An existing setting is modified: a prong style swapped, a band narrowed, a halo removed. The mold exists, but it gets altered before casting, or the CAD file for a stock design is edited rather than drawn fresh.

This is a legitimate middle ground and it is often the right answer. It is faster than fully custom and cheaper than most people assume. It just has a ceiling. You can move a design a certain distance from where it started, and past that distance, editing an existing file becomes slower and more error-prone than drawing a new one.

The three things sold as "custom," and what each one can do.
Ring builderSemi-customFully custom
Does a mold exist first?YesYes, then modifiedNo
What you chooseFrom a menuMenu plus adjustmentsEverything
Match a specific heirloom stoneOnly if it fits a stock sizeSometimesAlways
Fit a band flush to a curved ringNoRarelyYes
Typical waitDays to two weeksTwo to four weeksThree to six weeks
See it before it is madeStock renderingEdited CADCAD plus optional wax model

Is a custom engagement ring more expensive?

Usually not, and often the opposite. This surprises people, so it is worth explaining where a ring's money actually goes.

In a typical engagement ring, the center stone is 50 to 70 percent of the total, the metal and the labor of casting and setting are most of the rest, and the design work is a small slice of what remains. Drawing a setting from scratch adds hours of CAD time, not a different order of magnitude of cost. Meanwhile the thing that genuinely inflates a retail ring price is overhead: a lease, a sales floor, inventory that has been sitting in a case, and staff commission. A ring that has been sitting in a display case has been paid for by the store, insured by the store, and marked up to cover the months it did not sell.

That is why Ring Mint clients typically pay 30 to 50 percent less than the retail price of a comparable ring while getting a setting drawn for them specifically. There is no store, no showroom, no held inventory, no sales staff, and no separate design fee. The full breakdown is on the custom engagement rings page.

When is a ring builder the right choice?

When you like a stock setting and you need the ring quickly. I mean that sincerely. If you have found a solitaire in a builder that looks exactly right, and the proposal is in nine days, buying it is the correct decision and paying more for a custom version of the same silhouette would be a waste of money.

A builder is also the better call if the appeal for you is seeing the price update in real time as you change the stone. Custom does not work like that; the quote comes after a conversation, and some people find that uncomfortable. That is a real preference and it is worth respecting.

Where a builder fails is narrower than it sounds, but it fails completely. It cannot set a stone that is not a standard size. It cannot make a band that curves around another ring. It cannot make something that is not already in the catalog. If any of those describe what you want, no amount of filtering will get you there.

How to tell which one you are being sold

Four questions, and the answers are hard to fudge:

  • "Will I see a CAD render of my actual ring before it is made?" A builder shows you a stock rendering with your stone dropped in. Custom shows you a file of your ring, from any angle, with your measurements on it.
  • "Can I change the band width at the shoulders but not at the back?" A deliberately awkward request. Fully custom is a yes without hesitation. A configurator cannot do it and a semi-custom jeweler will tell you it depends on the base design, which is an honest answer.
  • "How many revisions do I get?" A fixed number usually means someone is editing a stock file and counting billable hours.
  • "Can I try it on before it is cast?" A mailed wax model is only possible when a file of your specific ring exists.

One thing from the bench: the request that most often forces a truly custom build is not an exotic design. It is an inherited stone. Old stones are cut to old proportions and almost never land on a modern standard size, so a catalog setting either does not close around them or holds them badly. That is when "customizable" runs out of room.

Related reading

  • What a fully custom engagement ring involves, step by step, including what is included and what it costs.
  • What an engagement ring concierge does, and how it compares with a configurator or a showroom.
  • Straight answers on budgets, timelines, deposits and sizing.

Quick answers

What is the difference between a custom and a customizable engagement ring?

A customizable ring, usually called a ring builder or a semi-mount, pairs your chosen center stone with a setting that already exists in the jeweler's catalog. Your choices come from a fixed menu: metal, stone shape, stone size, sometimes band width. A fully custom ring has no catalog behind it. The setting is modeled from scratch in CAD for one client, so every dimension is decided rather than selected.

Is a custom engagement ring more expensive than a ring builder?

Usually not. The center stone is 50 to 70 percent of a ring's cost and the metal and labor are most of the rest, so drawing a setting from scratch adds hours of CAD work rather than a different order of magnitude of cost. What actually inflates retail ring prices is overhead: a lease, a sales floor, held inventory and commission. A custom jeweler with no store typically comes in 30 to 50 percent below the retail price of a comparable ring.

What is a semi-mount?

A semi-mount is a finished setting made and stocked without a center stone, waiting for one to be set into it. Ring builders are built almost entirely from semi-mounts. It is a legitimate product and often the right one, but it means the design existed before you did.

Can a ring builder set an heirloom diamond?

Only if the heirloom happens to match a size the setting was made for. Older stones are cut to older proportions and rarely land on a modern standard measurement, so a stock setting either will not close around them or holds them insecurely. Resetting an inherited stone is one of the most common reasons a ring has to be built from scratch.

How do I know whether a jeweler is offering true custom?

Ask whether you will see a CAD render of your actual ring rather than a stock rendering, whether you can change one dimension in isolation (the band width at the shoulders but not at the back, for instance), how many revisions are included, and whether you can try a wax model on before anything is cast. Only a ring modeled from scratch can answer all four.
